content: Water fluoridation is the process of adding fluoride compounds to public water supplies with the goal of reducing tooth decay in the general population. This practice is widely implemented in many municipalities across North America and Australia, as it is believed to be a cost-effective method for improving dental health. In the United States, approximately 66% of residents who rely on public water systems receive fluoridated water. The fluoride compounds used in this process are often byproducts of phosphate ore processing, which is primarily conducted to produce fertilizers and food additives. Common fluoride compounds found in toothpaste include sodium fluoride (NaF), sodium monofluorophosphate (Na2FPO3), stannous fluoride (SnF2), and amine fluorides. The history of water fluoridation in the United States can be traced back to the early 20th century, particularly to the work of Dr. Frederick McKay. He investigated a condition known as Colorado brown stains, which caused discoloration and mottling of teeth in children from the Pikes Peak region. Despite the cosmetic impact, these children exhibited significantly fewer cavities compared to others. Dr. McKay collaborated with Dr. V. Black to further study this phenomenon, which eventually led to the identification of fluoride in the local water supply as the cause. The fluoride originated from the mineral cryolite in the region's rock formations, which dissolved into the water through rain and snow runoff. Subsequent research focused on determining a safe level of fluoride in drinking water to balance the prevention of dental caries with the risk of dental fluorosis. In 1934, Dr. H. Trendley Dean of the U.S. Public Health Service conducted a landmark epidemiological study involving 7,000 children across 21 cities. His findings, published in 1942, concluded that an optimal fluoride concentration of 1 part per million (ppm) minimized the risk of severe fluorosis while providing significant protection against tooth decay. In 1939, Dr. Gerald J. Cox proposed adding fluoride to drinking water to improve oral health, and by the mid-1940s, several studies were conducted to evaluate the effects of water fluoridation. Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city in the world to fluoridate its water supply on January 25, 1945, as part of a controlled study. Despite its widespread adoption, water fluoridation has been a source of controversy. Proponents argue that it is a public health measure comparable to fortifying salt with iodine, milk with vitamin D, or orange juice with vitamin C. They emphasize its effectiveness in preventing tooth decay. Opponents, however, raise concerns about potential health risks, such as dental fluorosis and bone cancer, and argue that fluoridation infringes on individual choice by imposing mass medication. The growing use of bottled water has raised concerns among dental professionals about reduced fluoride exposure. While some bottled water brands, such as Dannon, have begun adding fluoride, most do not, and fluoride concentrations are often not labeled. This trend may result in individuals consuming less fluoride than recommended, particularly if they rely on bottled water for cooking and drinking. Malfunctions in water fluoridation equipment have occasionally occurred, with one of the most severe incidents taking place in Hooper Bay, Alaska, in 1992. A failure in the fluoridation system led to the release of excessive fluoride into the drinking water, poisoning 296 people and causing one death. This marked the first reported fatality due to fluoride toxicity from a community water system. In the United States, the cost of water fluoridation varies by population size. In cities with over 50,000 residents, the cost is approximately 31 cents per person per year, while in smaller cities with populations under 10,000, the cost rises to $3.12 per person annually. As of 2002, 67% of Americans lived in communities with fluoridated water, and 19 states had at least 75% of their population receiving fluoridated water. In Canada, about 40% of the population receives fluoridated water, with implementation typically managed by provincial or city governments. Brantford, Ontario, was the first Canadian city to fluoridate its water in 1945. Toronto approved fluoridation in 1955 but delayed implementation until 1963 due to public opposition. British Columbia has historically had the lowest percentage of its population receiving fluoridated water, and Montreal remains one of the last major Canadian cities without fluoridated water. In Europe, water fluoridation is less common. In the United Kingdom, only 10% of the population receives fluoridated water, including residents of Birmingham and Newcastle upon Tyne. Spain permits fluoridation in some provinces, but coverage is limited to 10% of the population. France does not fluoridate its water supply, citing ethical and medical considerations, but fluoridated salt is widely available. Switzerland operated both water and salt fluoridation programs until 2003, when water fluoridation in Basel was discontinued to avoid overlap with fluoridated salt. In Oceania, Australia fluoridates water in all states except Queensland, where local governments control fluoridation. Brisbane, the state capital, does not fluoridate its water, although many regional centers in Queensland do. Beaconsfield, Tasmania, was the first Australian town to fluoridate its water in 1953. In New Zealand, nearly all water supplies are fluoridated except in remote areas. Fluoridation began in Hastings in 1954 and expanded rapidly after a 1957 Commission of Inquiry. Globally, South Africa supports water fluoridation, and approximately 45% of Brazilian cities have fluoridated water supplies, with studies reporting a 40–80% reduction in cavities among affected populations. In Israel, fluoridation began in 1981, and by 2002, over two million people (about one-third of the population) were receiving fluoridated water. In China, fluoride levels above 1 ppm are prohibited due to concerns about skeletal fluorosis.
